list.listitem: Any severe and recurrent headache is most likely to be a form of migraine and to be responsive to antimigraine therapy.B
Clinical features most predictive of migraine are nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, and exacerbation by physical activity.B

Neuroimaging should be considered in the presence of unexplained abnormal findings on neurologic examination B or atypical headache features or headaches that do not fulfill the strict definition of migraine or other primary headache disorder.C

Triptans (paired with an NSAID if tolerated) are first-line therapy for acute migraine treatment; rizatriptan 10 mg, eletriptan 80 mg, and almotriptan 12.5 mg provide the highest likelihood of consistent success.A

Lasmiditan, rimegepant, ubrogepant, and other calcitonin gene-related peptice (CGRP) antagonists are effective for acute migraine with or without aura in adults. No direct comparisons of either drug with triptans or other acute migraine therapies are available and the cost of these agents is high.A
First-line therapies for migraine prophylaxis in adults include propranolol, timolol, amitriptyline, divalproex sodium/sodium valproate, and topiramate.A

As second line therapies, four subcutaneously-injected anti-CGRP receptor monoclonal antibodies - eptinezumab, erenumab, fremanezumab, and galcanezumab - are approved for migraine prevention. Small molecule CGRP receptor antagonists are also effective as prophylactic agents.A

background.definition: Migraine is a common, multifactorial neurovascular disorder, typically presenting as recurrent disabling attacks of moderate to severe headache, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, and, in up to one-third of patients, neurologic aura symptoms.

list.listitem: Approximately 12% of the general population is affected (28-30 million migraine sufferers in the United States).
Lifetime prevalence is at least 18%.
Migraine is most common in those aged 30 to 39 years, in whom the prevalence in men and women reaches 7% and 24%, respectively.
The female to male ratio is 3:1.
Migraine is best understood as a primary disorder of the brain.
The basic biologic problem is dysfunction of an ion channel in the aminergic brainstem nuclei that normally modulate sensory input and exert neural influences on cranial vessels.
Familial predisposition exists, although specific genetic factors are not well characterized.
Migraine is a form of neurovascular headache: a disorder in which neural events result in the dilation of blood vessels, which in turn results in pain and further nerve activation.
Aura is characterized by a short phase of hyperemia (correlating with symptoms such as flashing and jagged lights) followed by a wave of oligemia that passes across the cortex at 2 to 6 mm/min.
Peripheral trigeminal nerve activation explains the common primary distribution of pain, with referred pain in the parietal, occipital, and high cervical regions.

Screening has been suggested by some researchers; 74% of consecutive patients who completed the Headache Assessment Quiz and screened positive were subsequently found to have migraine. Almost half of these patients had not been previously diagnosed with migraine. Of patients seen for any reason, 25% were found to have migraine. However, evidence-based guidelines and the United States Preventive Services Task Force do not recommend routine screening in the primary care setting.C
See the Treatment section for a discussion of migraine prophylaxis.
Diagnose migraine based on clinical history and physical examination consistent with International Headache Society (IHS) criteria ().C
Neurologic examination should be normal in patients with a diagnosis of migraine.C
The clinical features most predictive of migraine are nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, and exacerbation by physical activity.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pressure or tightness around both sides of the head or neck, nonthrobbing pain, not worsened by activity
Severe, debilitating headaches that occur repeatedly for weeks to months, followed by periods with no headache
Associated with at least two of the following: facial pain, pressure, congestion, nasal blockage, discharge or pus
Occurs in older patients and can be associated with fatigue, generalized aches and pain, night sweats, and vision loss

list.listitem: IHS criteria for diagnosis of migraine without aura are shown in .

In practice, diagnosis of migraine can be based on clinical history and physical examination consistent with the IHS criteria (), plus exclusion of secondary headache causes and other coexisting primary headache type.
Clinical features that are most predictive of migraine when present include nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, exacerbation by physical activity, and aura as triggers.

Signs and symptoms that are best at ruling out migraine include absence of nausea, photophobia, or physical activity as a trigger and absence of physical impairment due to headache in the past 3 months.

Evidence-based guidelines of the American Academy of Neurology suggest considering neuroimaging in nonacute headache patients with an unexplained abnormal finding on neurologic examination; atypical headache features or headaches that do not fulfill the strict definition of migraine or other primary headache disorder, or patients who have some additional risk factor, such as immune deficiency. See chapter on Headache (diagnosis) for more detailed information on initial assessment of undifferentiated headache.
EEG is not indicated in the routine evaluation of headache.

Symptoms shown to increase significantly the odds of finding a clinically pertinent abnormality on neuroimaging include: rapidly increasing headache frequency, history of dizziness or lack of coordination, history of subjective numbness or tingling, and history of headache causing awakening from sleep.
The limited number of available studies suggest that MRI may not be more sensitive than CT for identifying clinically significant pathology that is relevant to the cause of headache.
The POUND clinical decision rule is based on a study to identify the best independent predictors of migraine ().
The ID Migraine clinical decision rule is a prospectively validated tool ().

Suspect migraine in patients who report headache accompanied by nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, aggravation by physical activity, and aura. Validated clinical decision rules ( and ) can assist in the diagnosis.

Diagnosis is confirmed based on the history of at least five attacks fulfilling IHS criteria with history, physical examination, and neurologic examination that do not suggest any underlying organic disease.

Imaging should be considered for patients with nonacute headache and an abnormal neurologic examination; atypical headache features or headaches that do not fulfill the strict definition of migraine or other primary headache disorder; or some additional risk factor, such as immune deficiency.

Triptans (paired with an NSAID if tolerated) are first-line therapy for acute migraine treatment; rizatriptan 10 mg, eletriptan 80 mg, and almotriptan 12.5 mg provide the highest likelihood of consistent success.A

Lasmiditan, rimegepant, and ubrogepant are effective for acute migraine with or without aura in adults. No direct comparisons of these drugs with triptans or other acute migraine therapies are available.A

First-line therapies for migraine prophylaxis in adults include propranolol,timolol, amitriptyline, divalproex sodium/sodium valproate, and topiramate.A SSRIs and SNRIs are no more effective than placebo.

The subcutaneously-injected calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor antagonists eptinezumab, erenumab, fremanezumab, and galcanezumab are FDA-approved for migraine prevention. No comparative trials between these drugs and other preventive agents are available.A
Small molecule CGRP receptor antagonists ('the gepants") are also moderately effective for prophylaxis (NNT = 13).A

A comprehensive, high quality systematic review compared acute treatments for episodic migraine in adults. The strength of evidence is shown in parens for each comparison. They found that triptans and NSAIDs were more effective than placebo at 2 hours and 1 day (moderate to high). They also found that gepants (low to high), lasmiditan (high), dihydroergotamine (moderate to high), ergotamine + caffeine (moderate), acetaminophen (moderate), antiemetics (low), butorphanol (low), and tramadol + acetaminophen (low) significantly reduced pain. Adverse events were generally mild and transient. They found low quality or insufficient evidence regarding opioids, which are generally not recommended for treatment of migraine. Non-drug therapies that reduced pain included remote electrical neuromodulation (moderate), noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation (moderate), transcranial magnetic stimulation (low), and external trigeminal nerve stimulation (low).

A network meta-analysis identified 137 RCTs with 89,445 adults. They found that on average, triptans such as sumatriptan (Imitrex, Imigran, and others) and eletriptan (Relpax) are most likely to produce immediate relief of migraine pain and not require subsequent rescue medication.

The American College of Physicians commissioned a network meta-analysis and created a practice guidelines. Consistent with previous reviews, it found the strongest evidence for triptans. NSAID + triptan was more effective than triptan alone, but acetaminophen + triptan was not more effective. Their guideline recommends starting with an NSAID (if tolerated) or acetaminophen and adding a triptan as needed for moderate to severe acute episodic migraine.

Triptans are drugs of choice for treatment of acute migraine; NSAIDs and caffeine-containing combination analgesics are reasonable choices for mild-to-moderate migraine; ergot alkaloids may be considered in selected patients with moderate-to-severe migraine (). Acetaminophen is more effective than placebo, but inferior to other migraine therapies.
A meta-analysis of 53 trials showed that almotriptan 10 mg, eletriptan 80 mg, and rizatriptan 10 mg offer the highest likelihood of consistent success.

Compared with sumatriptan 100 mg: rizatriptan 10 mg shows better efficacy and consistency, and similar tolerability; eletriptan 80 mg shows better efficacy, similar consistency, but lower tolerability; almotriptan 12.5 mg shows similar efficacy at 2 hours but better sustained pain-free response, consistency, and tolerability; sumatriptan 25 mg, naratriptan 2.5 mg, and eletriptan 20 mg show lower efficacy and better tolerability; zolmitriptan 2.5 and 5 mg, eletriptan 40 mg, and rizatriptan 5 mg show very similar results.

A comparison study of sumatriptan 85 mg, naproxen sodium 500 mg, combination sumatriptan 85 mg/naproxen 500 mg, and placebo found superior 2- to 24-hour sustained pain-free response in the combination compared with either agent as monotherapy.

A case cross-over study found that patients were three times more likely to experience a stroke or MI if they had filled a new prescription for a triptan in the previous 2 weeks than if they hadn't (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.3 to 8.1) although absolute rates were quite low.
While effective, these agents should be considered second-line due to their high cost. In February, 2023 10 tablets of ubrogepant cost approximately $1000 (www.goodrx.com).

In a placebo-controlled RCT of 1672 adults with acute migraine with or without aura, oral ubrogepant 50 mg or 100 mg resulted in a 7.4% (50 mg) or 9.4% (100 mg) absolute increase in patients who were free from migraine pain at 2 hours compared to placebo (NNT = 10 to 13).

A second placebo-controlled RCT of ubrogepant for acute migraine included 1686 adults patients with 2 to 8 moderate or severe migraines per month. The NNT for freedom from pain at 2 hours was 13 (21% vs 14.3%).

In a crossover study (n=518), patients whose migraine prodromes accurately predict the onset of headaches had fewer moderate to severe headaches if they took ubrogepant during the prodrome than if they took placebo. The main outcome, the absence of a moderate to severe headache within 24 hours after taking the study drug, occurred in 28.6% of those taking placebo compared with 45.5% of those taking ubrogepant (NNT = 6; 95% CI 5 - 10). Adverse events were more common with ubrogepant (NNTH = 21, 95% CI 11-231).

Rimegepant (a calcitonin gene–related peptide receptor antagonist) was studied in a placebo-controlled RCT of 1186 patients for treatment of acute migraine. As in the studies of ubrogepant, it was moderately effective with NNT = 13 for freedom from pain at 2 hours. There are no comparisons with triptans or other medications for any of these new agents.

Atogepant was studied in a randomized trial with 873 patients given placebo or atogepant 10 mg, 30 mg, or 60 mg. Compared with placebo atogepant was only slightly more effective (1.2 to 1.7 fewer migraine days per month).

Intranasal zavegepant 10 mg was moderately superior to placebo in helping adults with acute migraine become pain free within 2 hours of treatment (NNT=12 for being pain free at 2 hours, NNT=17 for not needing rescue medication).

A systematic review identified 13 RCTs with 944 participants comparing ketorolac to other medications (phenothiazines, metoclopramide, sumatriptan, dexamethasone, sodium valproate, caffeine, and diclofenac). They concluded that ketorolac may provide better pain relief than sumatriiptan, sodium valproate, and dexamethasone. Otherwise there were no significant differences between it and other drugs. Small sample size may have hampered the ability to detect a true difference.
A trial randomized 56 children age 8 to 17 years presenting with acute migraine to IV ketorolac 0.5 mg/kg or intranasal ketorolac 1 mg/kg. Intranasal ketorolac was found to be non-inferior.

The subcutaneously-injected calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor antagonists include the monoclonal antibodies eptinezumab, erenumab, fremanezumab, and galcanezumab. They are FDA-approved for migraine prevention. No comparative trials between these drugs and other preventive agents are available.

The monoclonal antibody eptinezumab targets calcitonin gene-related peptide and was evaluated in a randomized trial with 480 patients for the acute treatment of moderate to severe migraine. Freedom from pain was faster with eptinezumab (4 vs 9 hours, p <0.001) and at 2 hours more patients were free of their most bothersome symptoms as well (23.5% vs 12.0%, p <0.001, NNT = 8).

Another randomized trial of eptinezumab randomized 891 persons to eptinezumab 300 mg, eptinezumab 100 mg, or placebo. Both dosages freduced the mean migraine days per month by approximately 3 days compared to placebo. Two participants experienced an anaphylactic reaction.

A trial comparing fremanezumab with placebo in 234 children 6 to 17 found that it slightly reduced migraine days (-2.5 vs -1.4, mean mean difference 1.1 days; 95% CI -1.9 to -0.2). Despite this fairly small mean difference of slightly more than a day, significantly more fremanezumab users had at least a 50% reduction in migraine days per month (47% vs 27%; P = .002; number needed to treat = 5).

An Italian cohort study followed 771 patients who took one of three monoclonal antibodies to CGRP (erenumab, fremanezumab or galcanezumab) for at least 24 weeks. After 12 weeks, 506 (65.6%) of the participants experienced at least a 50% reduction in the number of headache days. After 24 weeks, 146 (55.1%) of the 12-week nonresponders also had a 50% reduction in headache days. The late responders tended to have higher body mass index, more frequent treatment failures, more frequent psychiatric comorbidities, and allodynia.

In a randomized trial of 353 patients with migraine and comorbid depression, fremanezumab significantly reduced both depressive symptoms and the number of monthly migraine days. It is uncertain, however, whether a 1.4-point difference between fremanezumab and placebo in the HAM-D 17 depression rating tool at 8 weeks is clinically meaningful. The difference in depressive symptoms between fremanezumab and placebo was no longer significant at 12 weeks.

Metoclopramide 5 to 10 mg po/IM/IV may be considered as an adjunctive treatment to both decrease nausea and augment the analgesic effect of other agents. Prochlorperazine and chlorpromazine are also useful adjuncts in the treatment of nausea associated with migraine.

Added to standard treatment in the emergency department setting, dexamethasone (median dose 15 mg, given IV in 6 studies and orally in 1) reduced the likelihood of persistent or recurrent headache prompting return to the ED (NNT = 10).

A study randomized ED patients with acute migraine to IV magnesium, IV prochlorperazine, or IV magnesium. The average decreases on a 10 point numeric scale were 4 points, 3 points, and 4.5 points respectively with no significant difference between groups.

A crossover trial randomized patients to timolol eyedrops 0.5% or placebo for acute migraine, given at the onset of pain. The timolol-treated migraine attacks were more likely to result in a reduction in pain score by 4 points (on a 0 to 10 scale) or to 0 at 20 minutes than placebo (82% vs 14%, p <0.001, NNT = 2).

Ergot alkaloids, although long-standing components of treatment regimens, have very few randomized, placebo-controlled trials verifying their efficacy. Triptans show better efficacy; however, in some patients ergots offer a longer half-life and subsequently lower recurrence rates.

Two placebo-controlled RCTs including 3701 patients with episodic migraine demonstrated 50, 100 and 200 mg of lasmiditan, a serotonin 1F receptor agonist, was superior to placebo for both pain relief and pain freedom. Coadministration of lasmiditan with other serotonergic drugs, including triptans, may increase the risk of serotonin syndrome.
A small randomized trial of uncertain quality found a greater reduction in pain for patients with acute migraine with IV valproate than IV ibuprofen.

Generally accepted indications for preventative therapy include: (1) two or more migraines per month with disability lasting 3 or more days per month; (2) failure of, contraindication to, or adverse events from acute treatments; (3) use of abortive medication more than twice per week; and (4) uncommon migraine conditions, such as hemiplegic migraine or prolonged aura.

Initiate prophylactic therapy (see ) at low dose and titrate slowly, every 2 to 4 weeks; assess effectiveness after trial of at least 2 to 3 months. Successful therapy is generally defined as a reduction in migraine frequency by 50% (). Consider discontinuation of therapy after 6 to 12 months of effective treatment. Propranolol, timolol, divalproex sodium, and topiramate are Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved for migraine prevention. Propranolol and timolol have consistently demonstrated efficacy in clinical trials; other β-blockers have limited evidence to support efficacy. β-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (acebutolol, penbutolol, pindolol) are consistently ineffective for migraine prevention. A Cochrane review, which included 58 trials, concluded that propranolol is safe and effective but acknowledged methodologic shortcomings with some trials and a lack of long-term follow-up.

A network meta-analysis concluded that the medications most likely to be effective for prophylaxis in children were propranol and topiramate, although most studies were of short duration and the possibility of no effect could not be excluded.

Amitriptyline is the only antidepressant with consistent evidence supporting its effectiveness for migraine prevention. A Cochrane review found no evidence to support the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for migraine prophylaxis. Comparative study of propranolol and amitriptyline suggested that propranolol is more effective in patients with simple migraine and that amitriptyline is more beneficial for patients with mixed migraine and tension-type headache.
Candesartan has been demonstrated efficacy similar to propranolol in migraine prevention, but is not FDA-approved for this indication.

Divalproex sodium and sodium valproate are the most well-studied anticonvulsants for migraine prevention. A Cochrane review concluded that these agents are effective and suitable for routine clinical use, but they must be monitored for adverse effects.
Topiramate has demonstrated benefit in reducing migraine frequency in several clinical trials; comparisons with other, less expensive, prophylactic agents have not been done.

The subcutaneously-injected calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor antagonists erenumab, fremanezumab, and galcanezumab are FDA-approved for migraine prevention. No comparative trials between these drugs and other preventive agents are available. A post-hoc analysis of a large RCT concluded that erenumab was similarly effective for patients with migraine with and without aura.

In a placebo-controlled RCT of 875 adults with episodic migraine, subcutaneous fremanezumab administered monthly reduced the mean number of monthly migraine days after 12 weeks of follow-up, at an average drug cost of $7700/year. Subcutaneous erenumab has also demonstrated prophylactic effectiveness in a placebo-controlled RCT of 246 persons who had already failed 2-4 preventive strategies, at a similarly high cost. Another study randomized patients with chronic migraine to 140 mg eremumab, 70 mg, or placebo. Remission of medication use at 6 months occurrec in 69%, 60% and 52% respectively. Only the comparison with 140 mg was significant (NNT = 7). Although there have been no head-to-head trials, a network meta-analysis suggested that fremanezumab and erenumab are more effective than placebo, but not superior to propranolol or topiramate for reducing the number of migraine days.

Anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies were studied in a retrospective cohort study comparing 5153 patients who received one with 4000 who received control (botulinum toxin). There was no difference in cardiovascular events between groups.

A trial randomized 737 patients who had failed two other migraine preventive medicines to placebo or every other day rimegepant 75 mg. Patients had 10 headache days per month during a run-in phase. Rimegepant only reduced the number of headache days slightly more than placebo (4.3 vs 3.5 fewer days per month. While statistically significant, this is probably not clinically meaningful.

In another RCT, 778 patients with at least 15 migraines/month and who were highly adherent were randomized to atogepant 30 mg twice daily, atogepant 60 mg once daily + placebo once daily, or placebo twice daily. Migraine days decreased in all three groups, decreasing aboiut 2 days more than placebo for the atogepant groups.

OnabotulinumtoxinA, used as pericranial intramuscular injections, is FDA-approved for prevention of chronic migraine in adults. A Cochrane review concluded that the therapy may reduce the number of migraine days per month by 2, compared with placebo, but found the quality of limited evidence to be very low.

Numerous other medications have been studied for migraine prophylaxis, including: gabapentin, naproxen, timed-release dihydroergotamine (DHE), verapamil, magnesium, coenzyme Q10, and hormone therapy. Further evaluation of these agents is needed to determine their role in therapy.

Peripheral neurectomy is an option for selected patients with refractory migraine headache. In a small RCT of 26 patients in India with a good response to a bupivacaine block, surgery was more effective than continued medical therapy.

Implantable occipital nerve stimulators are recommended based on a review of 5 randomized clinical trials for patients with refractory chronic migraine by guidelines from the American Society of Pain and Neuroscience. A systematic review of 5 studies with 402 patients found a consistent reduction of 2.6 days (95% CI 0.9 to 4.3, I2 = 0%) compared with sham for occipital nerve stimulators.
A study comparing a greater occipital nerve block using bupivacaine 0.5% with metoclopramide in 99 ED patients with acute migraine found a slightly greater reduction in pain with metoclopramide.

Migraine is associated with patent foramen ovale. A pooled analysis of two studies with 337 patients randomizing them to a PFO Occluder device of medical treatment only. There was a small reduction in mean monthly migraine days (-3.1 vs. -1.9 days, p = 0.02) and a small number who became completely migraine free (9% vs 0.7%, p <0.001, NNT = 12). It is not possible to mask patients to treatment so placebo effect is a possibility.

A Cochrane review cited evidence suggesting that the addition of acupuncture to symptomatic treatment of migraine reduces the frequency of headaches. Acupuncture may be at least similarly effective as other prophylactic medications and may be an option for patients unwilling or unable to consider other pharmacologic options.

A randomized trial with 150 patients in China compared usual care with sham acupuncture with traditional acupuncture and found a reduction of 3.5 migraine days per month for traditional acupuncture, 2.4 for sham acupuncture, and 1.0 for usual care.

A meta-analysis of 31 RCTs found that prophylaxis with injections of botulinum toxin A led to about 2 fewer migraines per month compared to placebo. A 2018 Cochrane review confirms this finding but emphasizes the low quality of the limited evidence supporting botulinum toxin A in migraine prophylaxis.
There is conflicting evidence regarding the effectiveness of spinal manipulation for migraine prophylaxis.

A systematic review of 11 clinical trials found mixed results with high-dose riboflavin (vitamin B2, 400 mg daily) for migraine prophylaxis in adult patients. Therapy was generally well tolerated and inexpensive.

A Cochrane review identified six studies of feverfew involving 561 patients. Results were mixed and not convincing of efficacy; safety was good. A single, higher-quality study has demonstrated a reduction of 0.6 headaches per month with feverfew compared to placebo.
A systematic review found insufficient evidence to support using melatonin for migraine prophylaxis.
A systematic review of 3 small RCTs found some evidence supporting use of ginger for treatment of migraine, with slightly greater pain reduction at 2 hours.

In an open-label randomized study of 160 patients with episodic migraine at a single center in India with a high (29%) dropout rate, adding yoga to conventional medical therapy improved headache frequency, intensity, and migraine disability at 3 months of followup.
A systematic review of 6 randomized trials also found that yoga was associated with better outcomes, although the quality of included studies and the meta-analysis were both low.

In a randomized study of 98 patients with episodic migraines an average of 8 days in the preceding month, 16 weeks of mindfulness-based stress reduction classes reduced the number of headache days more than headache-specific stress management classes. However, by one year there was no difference in this outcome between groups. A second randomized trial found no difference between mindfulness based meditation and migraine education on the primary outcome of migraine days, but did find improvements in some secondary outcomes related to disability, quality of life, depression, self-efficacy and catastrophizing. More study is needed.
Monitor patients' headaches with a headache diary. Diaries should record headache frequency, severity, duration, disability, response to therapy, and adverse effects of medication.

Regular sleep, regular meals, exercise, avoidance of peaks of stress and troughs of relaxation, and avoidance of apparent dietary triggers may help decrease migraine frequency. The patient should aim for regularity of habits, rather than to adhere to a list of prohibited foods and activities.

Patent foramen ovale (PFO) has been associated with migraine, particularly migraine with aura. Observational evidence suggests that patients undergoing PFO closure for other indications, and who also have migraine, may see a reduction in their migraine frequence and severity. Current evidence does not support offering PFO closure solely for the purpose of migraine prevention.
Hyperbaric oxygen may be helpful for termination of acute migraine, but studies are small and generally of poor quality.

In patients with acute migraine, a TENS unit was more effective than a sham TENS in a randomized trial with 83 adults aged 18 to 50 years. The pain reduction was 65 mm for TENS and 9 mm for sham, and 30 patients in the sham group required rescue analgesics compared to only 1 in the TENS group.

A randomized trial of adults with frequent migraine found that adding omega-3 fatty acids to the diet, or better yet substituting omega-6 fatty acids with omega 3's, reduced headache days by 2 to 4 days per month. However, vitamin D 2000 IU/day and omega n-3 fatty acid 1 gram/day both had no effect on patient report of migraine frequency in the VITAL trial with 25,871 participants. This study used oral supplements rather than dietary substitution.

In this industry-funded RCT with 144 patients, an investigational, proprietary, vibrating intranasal ballon catheter decreased short-term headache frequency in adults with chronic migraine more than a sham device, but with a high rate of adverse effects.
The most effective prophylactic agents reduce headaches by 20% to 50% compared with placebo; 10% or less will become headache free.B

A prospective cohort study of 20,084 men from the Physicians' Health Study found that men who self-reported migraine had multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios of 1.24 for major cardiovascular disease and 1.42 for myocardial infarction. In migraineurs younger than 55, the age-adjusted hazard ratio of ischemic stroke was 1.84; there was no significant association in the older age groups. The study did not collect information on migraine aura or on the use of migraine-specific drugs.B
Migraine frequency tends to decrease after the age of 50 years in both men and women.
Choice of agent for acute and prophylactic treatment is based on comorbidities, contraindications, and potential adverse effects.
Consider first-line prophylactic agents; amitriptyline should generally be avoided.
There are no specific clinical trials evaluating drug treatment of migraine during pregnancy.

Most migraine medications, including triptans and ergot alkaloids, are contraindicated in pregnancy. However, sumatriptan has a large pregnancy register with no reports of any adverse events or complications that might be attributed to sumatriptan.
Many migraneurs experience fewer or no attacks during pregnancy.

The American Academy of Neurology guidelines recommend ibuprofen or acetaminophen for children, while adolescents do better with triptans. Some adolescents can experience complete relief after two hours using oral sumatriptan plus naproxen or with sumatriptan nasal spray. The most robust data for chemoprophylaxis are on propranolol and it appears to be only slightly better than placebo. Amitriptyline plus cognitive behavioral therapy appears to be the most effective approach to decreasing headache frequency, but these data are limited to just a single study.

A meta-analysis of 12 RCTs with 576 children evaluated non-pharmacologic treatments for decreasing migraine frequency. They found evidence to support the use of biofeedback, relaxation techniques, and general or specific psychological support (eg, cognitive behavioral therapy).

Sumatriptan nasal spray is the only triptan with positive placebo-controlled trials in the treatment of acute migraine in children and adolescents; the recommended dose for children of 12 years and older is 10 mg.
Oral triptans did not show significant efficacy in placebo-controlled childhood and adolescent studies.

A Cochrane review concluded that there is little evidence to guide the choice of drugs for migraine prophylaxis in children. Topiramate and amitriptyline were no more effective than placebo in reducing migraine frequency or disability in a RCT, although children in all 3 groups demonstrated substantial improvement.

A network meta-analysis concluded that the medications most likely to be effective for migraine prophylaxis in children were propranol and topiramate, although most studies were of short duration and the possibility of no effect could not be excluded.

Another network meta-analysis identified 45 studies with 2617 patients and concluded that pregabalin, topiramate with or without vitamin D, flunarizine, levetiracetam, riboflavin, cinnarizine, and amitriptyline were associated with reduced migraine frequency. Propranolol and cinnarizine, pregabalin, valproate, levetiracetam, and cinnarizine significantly reduced migraine intensity. However, no treatments were associated with a significant reduction in disability or improved quality of life.
A trial randomized 56 children age 8 to 17 years presenting with acute migraine to IV ketorolac 0.5 mg/kg or intranasal ketorolac 1 mg/kg. Intranasal ketorolac was found to be non-inferior.

A trial comparing fremanezumab with placebo in 234 children 6 to 17 found that it slightly reduced migraine days (-2.5 vs -1.4, mean mean difference 1.1 days; 95% CI -1.9 to -0.2). Despite this fairly small mean difference of slightly more than a day, significantly more fremanezumab users had at least a 50% reduction in migraine days per month (47% vs 27%; P = .002; number needed to treat = 5).

algorithm.title: Suggested Algorithm for Selecting Migraine Prophylaxis.

cell.label: Patient candidate for pharmacologic migraine prophylaxis (e.g., 2 migraine/mo, 3 mo disability 3 disability d/mo)
Consider a first-line agent, if no contraindication: Propranolol or timolol; amitriptyline; divalproex sodium or sodium valproate; topiramate.
Schedule regular follow-up visits to monitor medication use.
Adjust dose as tolerated. If adverse effects or ineffective try different first-line agent (propranolol or timolol, amitriptyline, divalproex, or topiramate). Effective after 2-3 mo?
If no single first-line drug is effective and tolerable, consider a combination of two first-line agents. Effective after 2-3 mo?

Consider an alternative agent, if no contraindications: Gabapentin; naproxen sodium; candesartan; lisinopril; atenolol, metoprolol, or nadolol; magnesium; riboflavin (B2) or coenzyme Q10; hormone therapy; timed-released DHE; verapamil; feverfew.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Migraine Without Aura (2004 International Headache Society Classification).

list.listitem: At least five attacks fulfilling criteria B-D
Headache lasting 4-72 h (untreated or unsuccessfully treated)

Headache has at least two of the following characteristics: Unilateral location Pulsating quality Moderate or severe pain intensity Aggravation by or causing avoidance of routine physical activity (eg, walking or climbing stairs)
During headache at least one of the following: Nausea and/or vomiting Photophobia and phonophobia
Not attributed to another disorder
